who: David was a shepherd from Bethlehem, the youngest son of Jesse. The prophet Samuel anointed him while Saul was still king. He killed Goliath and fled from Saul for years. Then he reigned forty years, most of them in Jerusalem. He sinned with Bathsheba and repented. Many psalms bear his name, and Jesus is called the Son of David.

tidbits.text: No one else in the whole Bible is called David. The name belongs to the king alone, says the *Catholic Encyclopedia*.

At the cave of Adullam he longed for water from the well by Bethlehem's gate. Three of his mighty men broke through the Philistine camp to fetch it. He poured it out to the LORD instead: “Is this not the blood of the men who risked their lives?”

The Fathers read his life as a picture of Christ's, says the *Catholic Encyclopedia*. The shepherd of Bethlehem pointed to the Good Shepherd, and his five stones to the five wounds. Fleeing his son, he crossed the Kidron Valley, as Jesus did on the night He was betrayed.
Psalm 72 ends, “Thus conclude the prayers of David son of Jesse.” Yet more psalms headed with his name come later in the book.

facts.label: Born
facts.text: In **Bethlehem** of Judah, the youngest son of **Jesse**. He was thirty when he became king. The Missouri Synod dates his reign **about 1010 to 970 BC**.

facts.label: Family
facts.text: His father **Jesse** was the grandson of **Ruth** and Boaz. His sister **Zeruiah** was the mother of Joab. His wives included Saul's daughter **Michal**, **Abigail** and **Bathsheba**. Chronicles names **nineteen sons**, among them **Absalom** and **Solomon**, and a daughter, **Tamar**.

facts.label: Work
facts.text: A **shepherd**, then Saul's **harpist** and armour-bearer, a **commander** in his army, an **outlaw** captain, and **king**.

facts.label: Anointed
facts.text: **Three times**: by Samuel at Bethlehem, by the men of Judah at Hebron, and by the elders of all Israel at Hebron.

facts.label: Capital
facts.text: **Jerusalem**. He took its fortress, Zion, from the Jebusites and named it **the City of David**.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **The son of Jesse**. **The sweet psalmist of Israel**, in his last words. **The Prophet-King**, in the Orthodox Church. **King and prophet**, in the *Roman Martyrology*.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: In **Jerusalem**, at **seventy**, after forty years as king.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: In **the City of David**. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* places the grave on **Mount Zion**. Josephus says great riches were buried with him.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: **73 psalms** are headed with his name in the Hebrew Bible. The Missouri Synod calls him “the author of no less than 73 psalms”. His laments for Saul and Jonathan and for Abner, a song of victory and his last words are in 2 Samuel. More on the psalms below.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: With a **harp** and a crown. As a young man, with a **sling**, or with Goliath's sword.

moments.title: Anointed among his brothers
moments.text: God sent the prophet Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint one of Jesse's sons as king. Samuel saw the eldest, Eliab, and thought this must be the one. But the LORD said, “Do not consider his appearance or height.” And then: “For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart.” Seven sons passed before Samuel, and none was chosen. “There is still the youngest,” Jesse said, “but he is tending the sheep.” They sent for David, and Samuel anointed him in front of his brothers. “And the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward.”

moments.title: The harp
moments.text: A spirit of distress tormented King Saul, and his servants looked for someone who could play the harp. One of them knew a son of Jesse: “a mighty man of valor, a warrior, eloquent and handsome, and the LORD is with him.” So David came to court. Saul loved him very much and made him his armour-bearer. Whenever the distress came on Saul, David took up his harp and played. “Then Saul would find relief and feel better.”

moments.title: Goliath
moments.text: The Philistine champion, Goliath of Gath, came out every morning and evening to challenge Israel, and no one would face him. David came to the camp with bread for his brothers, and heard him. “You are just a boy,” Saul said. But David had killed lions and bears to save his father's sheep. He tried on Saul's armour, but could not walk in it. He chose five smooth stones from the brook and ran toward the battle line. “The battle is the LORD's,” he told Goliath. His stone sank into the giant's forehead, “and he fell facedown on the ground.”

moments.title: Saul's spear
moments.text: The women came out dancing and singing: “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.” Saul was furious. “What more can he have but the kingdom?” From that day he kept a jealous eye on David. While David played the harp, Saul hurled his spear at him, twice. Later Saul sent men to kill him at home. David's wife Michal, Saul's daughter, let him down through a window. Then she laid a household idol in his bed, with goat hair on its head.

moments.when: The feast of the New Moon
moments.title: Jonathan's arrows
moments.text: Saul's son Jonathan loved David “as himself”. He promised to learn whether his father meant to kill him. David would hide in a field. Jonathan would shoot arrows and call to the boy who ran for them. If he called out that the arrows were beyond him, David must flee. Saul did mean it. Jonathan shot, and called, “Isn't the arrow beyond you?” When the boy had gone, the two friends “kissed each other and wept together—though David wept more.”

moments.title: The holy bread
moments.text: David fled to the priests at Nob. He asked the priest Ahimelech for five loaves. There was no bread but the consecrated bread, taken from before the LORD, and the priest gave it to him. There too, wrapped in a cloth, was the sword of Goliath. “There is none like it,” David said. “Give it to me.” Jesus later reminded the Pharisees of that day: “Have you not read what David did when he and his companions were hungry?”

moments.place: Gath, then the cave of Adullam
moments.title: A madman, then a captain
moments.text: He fled to Gath, Goliath's own city, and its king's servants knew him. So he pretended to be mad. He scratched on the doors of the gate “and let his saliva run down his beard.” The king drove him away. He hid in the cave of Adullam, and his family came to him there. “And all who were distressed or indebted or discontented rallied around him, and he became their leader.” There were about four hundred of them. The headings of Psalm 34 and Psalm 142 set those psalms in these days.

moments.when: Saul hunts him with three thousand men
moments.title: The corner of Saul's robe
moments.text: Saul went into a cave, not knowing that David and his men were hiding deep inside it. David's men said this was the day God had promised him. David crept up and cut off a corner of Saul's robe. Then his conscience struck him. “The LORD forbid that I should do such a thing to my master, the LORD's anointed.” When Saul left, David called out after him and bowed to the ground. He showed him the corner of his robe. Saul wept aloud. “You are more righteous than I.”

moments.title: Abigail
moments.text: David's men had guarded the flocks of a rich man named Nabal. When they asked him for food, Nabal sneered, “Who is David?” David told his men to strap on their swords. Nabal's wife Abigail, “an intelligent and beautiful woman”, loaded donkeys with bread, wine, meat, raisins and figs, and rode out to meet him. She fell at his feet and took the blame. David blessed God, and blessed her: “Blessed is your discernment, and blessed are you, because today you kept me from bloodshed and from avenging myself by my own hand.” Ten days later Nabal died, and David asked Abigail to be his wife.

moments.title: “How the mighty have fallen!”
moments.text: Saul and Jonathan died fighting the Philistines on Mount Gilboa. When the news came, David tore his clothes, and he and his men wept and fasted until evening. He wrote a lament for them, the Song of the Bow. “How the mighty have fallen!” it cries, three times. Of his friend he wrote, “I grieve for you, Jonathan, my brother.” Then the men of Judah came to Hebron and anointed David king.

moments.title: The City of David
moments.text: He was thirty when he became king. He reigned in Hebron over Judah for seven and a half years. Then all the tribes came to him: “Here we are, your own flesh and blood.” They anointed him king over all Israel. He marched on Jerusalem, whose people boasted that even the blind and lame could keep him out. He took the fortress of Zion, named it the City of David, and made it his capital.

moments.title: Dancing before the LORD
moments.text: David brought the ark of God up to his city with shouting and the sound of the ram's horn. Wearing a linen ephod, he “danced with all his might before the LORD”. His wife Michal watched from a window and despised him. She mocked the show he had made of himself before the servant girls. “I was dancing before the LORD,” he told her. “I will celebrate before the LORD, and I will humiliate and humble myself even more than this.”

moments.when: A word to Nathan by night
moments.title: A house for God
moments.text: “Here I am, living in a house of cedar,” David said, “while the ark of God remains in a tent.” He wanted to build God a temple. That night God sent the prophet Nathan back with a promise. David would not build a house for God. God would build a house for David, a line of kings: “Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me, and your throne will be established forever.” David went in and sat before the LORD. “Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?” Later he told Solomon why he could not build it: God had said to him, “You have shed much blood.”

moments.when: In the spring, when kings march out to war
moments.title: Bathsheba and Uriah
moments.text: David sent his army to war and stayed in Jerusalem. From the palace roof he saw a very beautiful woman bathing. She was Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, one of his soldiers. David sent for her and slept with her, and she conceived. He called Uriah home from the war, but Uriah would not go to his own house while the army camped in the open field. So David sent him back with a letter for Joab: “Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest battle.” Uriah was killed, and David married Bathsheba. “But the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD.”

moments.title: “You are that man!”
moments.text: The LORD sent Nathan to David with a story. A rich man had many flocks. When a traveller came, he did not take one of his own sheep. He took a poor man's only lamb, a pet that “was like a daughter to him”, and served it. David burned with anger. “The man who did this deserves to die!” Nathan said, “You are that man!” David said, “I have sinned against the LORD.” Nathan replied, “The LORD has taken away your sin.” But the child would die. David fasted and lay on the ground for seven days. When the child died, he got up, washed and worshipped. “I will go to him, but he will not return to me.”

moments.title: Barefoot and weeping
moments.text: His son Absalom stole the hearts of Israel and had himself proclaimed king in Hebron. David fled Jerusalem. He crossed the Kidron Valley and went up the Mount of Olives, “weeping as he went up”, barefoot, his head covered. On the road a man of Saul's family, Shimei, threw stones and cursed him. Abishai offered to cut off his head. David said, “Leave him alone and let him curse me, for the LORD has told him so.”

moments.title: “My son, my son”
moments.text: David's army met Absalom's in the forest of Ephraim. The king had ordered his commanders, “Treat the young man Absalom gently for my sake.” Riding under a large oak, Absalom caught his head fast in its branches, and his mule went on without him. Joab found him hanging there and killed him. When David heard, he went up to the room over the gate and wept: “O my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!”

moments.when: After the count of the people
moments.title: “Offerings that cost me nothing”
moments.text: David ordered his fighting men counted. Joab tried to talk him out of it. Afterward David's conscience struck him: “I have sinned greatly in what I have done.” A plague fell on the land. When David saw the angel striking the people, he prayed, “Surely I, the shepherd, have sinned and acted wickedly. But these sheep, what have they done?” He was told to build an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah. Araunah offered it as a gift. David would not take it: “I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing.” There the plague stopped. There, too, Solomon later built the temple.

words.note: He wrote no book of his own. His words are kept in Samuel, Kings and Chronicles, and in the psalms headed with his name. Outside the quiz's own section, every Bible line on this page is from the Berean Standard Bible. The exceptions are Sirach and Psalm 151, from the World English Bible.

extras.title: The psalms of David
extras.lede: Seventy-three psalms carry David's name in their Hebrew headings. Did he write those, or all 150, or fewer? Jews and Christians have answered in different ways. Here each speaks for itself.

items.title: What the headings say
items.text: The headings are part of the Bible's text. In the Hebrew Bible 73 name David, and the Greek names him in many more, says the *Catholic Encyclopedia*. Some tie a psalm to a day in his life: Psalm 3 to his flight from Absalom, Psalm 51 to Nathan's visit. The New Testament gives him some psalms that have no heading, like Psalm 2 and Psalm 95. The Greek Bible even adds a Psalm 151, “outside the number”, and heads it as David's own. Jesus Himself quoted Psalm 110 as David's:
items.quote: Speaking by the Holy Spirit, David himself declared: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand until I put Your enemies under Your feet.”’

items.title: The Talmud
items.text: The Talmud names who wrote each book of the Bible. It gives the psalms to David with ten others: Adam, Melchizedek, Abraham, Moses, Heman, Jeduthun, Asaph and the three sons of Korah. Another passage gives them all to David, says the *Catholic Encyclopedia*.
items.quote: David wrote Psalms, with the assistance of ten elders

cite.text: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 14b, tr. Michael Rodkinson; Catholic Encyclopedia, “Psalms”

items.title: Augustine: all 150
items.text: The early Church was divided too. Augustine knew readers who gave David only the psalms headed with his name. He held that David wrote the whole book, and set other men's names over some psalms as God inspired him. Ambrose held the same, says the *Catholic Encyclopedia*.
items.quote: those seem to me to hold the more credible opinion, who ascribe to him the authorship of all these hundred and fifty psalms

cite.text: Augustine, *City of God*, book 17, chapter 14; Catholic Encyclopedia, “Psalms”

items.title: Jerome: not all
items.text: Jerome disagreed, and so did Origen, Hilary and Eusebius, says the *Catholic Encyclopedia*. For them a psalm headed with another name, Asaph's or the sons of Korah's, was that man's work. Jerome said so in a letter:
items.quote: they err who deem all the psalms are David's and not the work of those whose names are superscribed

cite.text: Jerome, Letter 140, as the Catholic Encyclopedia gives it

items.title: Rome, in 1910
items.text: The Council of Trent called the book {la|Psalterium Davidicum}, the Psalter of David. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* says Trent meant to settle nothing about who wrote it. In 1910 Rome's Biblical Commission ruled that David need not be held the author of every psalm. But it also ruled:
items.quote: It cannot be prudently denied that David is the chief author of the songs of the Psalter.

cite.text: Pontifical Biblical Commission, 1 May 1910, as the Catholic Encyclopedia gives it

items.title: Scholars today
items.text: Scholars today believe the book gathers psalms from every period of Israel's history, from before the kings to after the Exile, says *Britannica*. *Britannica* sums it up:
items.quote: The dating of individual psalms poses an extremely difficult problem, as does the question of their authorship.

myths.claim: Goliath was over nine feet tall.
myths.truth: The standard Hebrew text says so: “six cubits and a span”, about 9 feet 9 inches. But the Greek Septuagint, the Dead Sea Scrolls and Josephus all give “four cubits and a span”, about 6 feet 9 inches. That is still a giant of a soldier. *Britannica* calls him “a sizable man, but not improbably tall”.

cite.text: 1 Samuel 17:4, with the Bible Hub footnote; Josephus, Antiquities, book 6, chapter 9; Britannica, “How Tall Was Goliath in the Bible?”

myths.claim: Bathsheba set out to tempt the king.
myths.truth: The Bible does not say so. It says David stayed home from the war, saw her bathing from his palace roof, asked who she was, and “sent messengers to get her”. Nathan's story of the stolen lamb is aimed at David, and so is the verdict: “the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD.”

myths.claim: Absalom hung from a tree by his long hair.
myths.truth: 2 Samuel says his head was caught fast in the branches of an oak. His hair is told of earlier: he cut it once a year, when it grew too heavy, and it weighed two hundred shekels. Josephus, writing about 93, joined the two. He says Absalom “entangled his hair greatly in the large boughs of a knotty tree”.

myths.claim: The Star of David was David's own sign.
myths.truth: The Bible never mentions it. The *Jewish Encyclopedia* notes that “the shield of David is not mentioned in rabbinical literature”. The oldest Jewish book it knew to name the sign was written in the 1100s. In 1354 the Jews of Prague were given a red flag that bore it. Today it is the symbol of Judaism.

circle.name: Ruth
circle.text: His great-grandmother, a woman of Moab. Her son Obed “became the father of Jesse, the father of David.”

circle.name: Jonathan
circle.text: Saul's son and David's closest friend. On the day they met, he gave David his own robe, tunic, sword, bow and belt. He died beside his father on Mount Gilboa.

circle.name: Abigail
circle.text: The wise wife of Nabal. She rode out with food and kept David from taking revenge. After Nabal died she became David's wife, and bore him a son, Chileab.

circle.name: Saul
circle.text: Israel's first king. He loved David at first and made him his armour-bearer. Then the women's song made him jealous, and he hunted David for years. Wounded on Mount Gilboa, he fell on his own sword.

circle.name: Samuel
circle.text: The prophet who anointed him at Bethlehem. When David first fled from Saul, he ran to Samuel at Ramah.

circle.name: Michal
circle.text: Saul's daughter, who loved David and became his first wife. She saved his life through a window. Saul then gave her to another man, and David later took her back. When he danced before the ark, she despised him.

circle.name: Bathsheba
circle.text: The wife of Uriah the Hittite, and after his death David's wife. She was the mother of Solomon. In David's old age she and Nathan made sure Solomon took the throne. Matthew's list of Jesus' ancestors names her as Uriah's wife.

circle.name: Nathan
circle.text: The prophet who brought him God's promise of a lasting house. Later he told him the story of the poor man's lamb: “You are that man!” He helped to crown Solomon.

circle.name: Joab
circle.text: His nephew, the son of his sister Zeruiah, and the commander of his army. He led David's wars and carried out the order against Uriah. He also killed Abner, Absalom and Amasa. “These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too fierce for me,” David said.

circle.name: Absalom
circle.text: His third son, the most handsome man in Israel. He had his half-brother Amnon killed, for Amnon had violated his sister Tamar. Later he turned Israel's hearts to himself and rose against his father. He died in the forest of Ephraim.

circle.name: Solomon
circle.text: His son by Bathsheba. Nathan named him Jedidiah, “because the LORD loved him.” David had him anointed king before he died. Solomon built the temple David had planned.

circle.name: Mephibosheth
circle.text: Jonathan's son, lame in both feet. For Jonathan's sake David gave him back Saul's land. He ate at the king's table “like one of the king's own sons.”

death.big: He died in Jerusalem at seventy, after forty years as king. He was buried in the City of David.
paras: In his old age his son Adonijah declared, “I will be king!” Nathan and Bathsheba reminded David of his oath. That same day he had Solomon anointed, and the people shouted, “Long live King Solomon!”
As the time drew near for him to die, he charged Solomon to keep the Law of Moses. He also named men to reward and men to punish, among them Joab, and Shimei, who had cursed him on the road.
“Then David rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David.” Chronicles adds that he died “at a ripe old age, full of years, riches, and honor.”

At Pentecost, Peter reminded Jerusalem that “the patriarch David died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day.” David was a prophet, Peter said. In his psalm he spoke of the Christ, Whose body would not see decay.

items.q: The Spirit of the LORD spoke through me; His word was on my tongue.
items.ctx: “These are the last words of David,” says 2 Samuel. In them he calls himself “the sweet psalmist of Israel”.

items.k: On a king who rules well
items.q: He who rules the people with justice, who rules in the fear of God, is like the light of the morning at sunrise of a cloudless dawn
I am about to go the way of all the earth. So be strong and prove yourself a man.

later.title: The treasure in the tomb
later.text: Josephus says David “had great and immense wealth buried with him”. By his count, “a thousand and three hundred years afterward” the high priest Hyrcanus was besieged by a king named Antiochus. He opened one room of the tomb, took out three thousand talents, and paid Antiochus part of it to lift the siege. Later King Herod opened another. But “neither of them came at the coffins of the kings themselves”.

cite.text: Josephus, Antiquities, book 7, chapter 15, tr. William Whiston

saint.big: Yes, as a king and prophet. He is honoured as a saint in the Orthodox and Catholic calendars.

churches.note: Not in the English or Episcopal calendars

paras: The OCA calls him “a forefather of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh”. His great sin darkened his life, it says. “He was also an example of great repentance.”
The Coptic synaxarium says “God was with him in all his ways, for his purity of heart and his meekness.”
The Missouri Synod's calendar finds his greatness in his loyalty to God, “coupled with his willingness to acknowledge his sins and ask for God's forgiveness”.

kin.name: Augustine of Hippo
kin.text: Dying, he had the shortest penitential psalms of David copied out and hung on the wall by his bed. He read them, and “wept freely and constantly”.
